text: The very fact. <break time="0.8s" /> That all of our experiences take place in a physical space. <break time="0.8s" /> Makes the space inseparable. <break time="0.8s" /> From what defines it. <break time="0.8s" /> From the event that took place in it. <break time="0.8s" /> The tree and the ground beneath. <break time="0.8s" /> Are inseparable. <break time="0.8s" /> From what took place there. <break time="0.8s" /> This intertwining of space, place, and experience. <break time="0.8s" /> Challenges the idea of place as passive backdrop. <break time="0.8s" /> If place and space are central. <break time="0.8s" /> To the very heart of experience. <break time="0.8s" /> We must accept the possibility. <break time="0.8s" /> That the spatial framework is the medium of all experiences. <break time="0.8s" /> , actions, thoughts, memories, and feelings of every place. <break time="0.8s" /> Not merely a background or context exterior to experience. <break time="0.8s" /> As commonly supposed. <break time="0.8s" /> Belgian literary critic Georges Poulet. <break time="0.8s" /> Made the point elegantly. <break time="0.8s" /> Writing of the space. <break time="0.8s" /> Created in Marcel Prousts great novel In Search of Lost Time. <break time="0.8s" /> Beings surround themselves. <break time="0.8s" /> With the places where they find themselves. <break time="0.8s" /> The way one wraps oneself up in a garment. <break time="0.8s" /> That is at one and the same time a disguise. <break time="0.8s" /> And a characterization. <break time="0.8s" /> Without places. <break time="0.8s" /> Beings would be only abstractions.
